- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.

####################################################################################
####################################################################################
## Copyright (c) 2018 - 2021 Analog Devices, Inc.
### SPDX short identifier: BSD-1-Clause
## Auto-generated, do not modify!
####################################################################################
####################################################################################

include quiet.mk

help:
	@echo ""
	@echo "Please specify a target."
	@echo ""
	@echo "To make all projects:"
	@echo "    make all"
	@echo ""
	@echo "To build a specific project:"
	@echo "    make proj.board"
	@echo "e.g.,"
	@echo "    make adv7511.zed"


PROJECTS := $(filter-out $(NO_PROJ), $(notdir $(wildcard projects/*)))
SUBPROJECTS := $(foreach projname,$(PROJECTS), \
	$(if $(wildcard projects/$(projname)/system_project.tcl), $(projname) , \
	$(foreach archname,$(notdir $(subst /Makefile,,$(wildcard projects/$(projname)/*/Makefile))), \
		$(projname).$(archname))))

.PHONY: lib all clean clean-ipcache clean-all $(SUBPROJECTS)

$(SUBPROJECTS):
	$(MAKE) -C projects/$(subst .,/,$@)

lib:
	$(MAKE) -C library/ all


all:
	$(MAKE) -C projects/ all


clean:
	$(MAKE) -C projects/ clean

clean-ipcache:
	$(call clean, \
		ipcache, \
		$(HL)IP Cache$(NC))

clean-all:clean clean-ipcache
	$(MAKE) -C projects/ clean
	$(MAKE) -C library/ clean

####################################################################################
####################################################################################

===project-xilinx.mk===
####################################################################################
## Copyright (c) 2018 - 2023, 2025 Analog Devices, Inc.
## SPDX short identifier: BSD-1-Clause
####################################################################################

# Assumes this file is in projects/scripts/project-xilinx.mk
HDL_PROJECT_PATH := $(subst scripts/project-xilinx.mk,,$(lastword $(MAKEFILE_LIST)))
HDL_LIBRARY_PATH := $(HDL_PROJECT_PATH)../library/

include $(HDL_PROJECT_PATH)../quiet.mk

# Parse the config file and convert it to environment variables
PARAMS_REPLACE_LIST := JESD LANE # list of words that should be removed from the parameter names
GEN_SED := '$(foreach name, $(PARAMS_REPLACE_LIST), s/$(name)//g;);s/_//g'
ifdef CFG
    include $(CFG)
    export $(shell sed 's/=.*//' $(CFG) | tr '\n' ' ')
    PARAMS := $(shell cat $(CFG) | tr '\n' ' ')
    DIR_NAME := $(basename $(notdir $(CFG)))
endif

VIVADO := vivado -tempDir .Xil -mode batch -source

# Parse the variables passed to make and convert them to the filename format
ifeq ($(shell expr $(MAKELEVEL) % 2),0)
  CMD_VARIABLES := $(shell echo $(-*-command-variables-*-) | tac -s ' ')
else
  CMD_VARIABLES := $(shell echo $(MAKEOVERRIDES))
endif

ifneq ($(strip $(CMD_VARIABLES)), )
    PARAMS := $(shell echo $(CMD_VARIABLES) | sed -e 's/[=]/_/g')
    GEN_NAME := $(shell echo $(PARAMS) | sed -e $(GEN_SED) | sed -e 's/[ .]/_/g')
    DIR_NAME := $(if $(strip $(DIR_NAME)),$(DIR_NAME)_$(GEN_NAME),$(GEN_NAME))
endif

ifneq ($(strip $(DIR_NAME)), )
    PROJECT_NAME := $(DIR_NAME)/$(PROJECT_NAME)
    $(shell test -d $(DIR_NAME) || mkdir $(DIR_NAME))
    ADI_PROJECT_DIR := $(DIR_NAME)/
    export ADI_PROJECT_DIR
	VIVADO := vivado -tempDir $(DIR_NAME)/.Xil -log $(DIR_NAME)/vivado.log -journal $(DIR_NAME)/vivado.jou -mode batch -source
endif

CLEAN_TARGET := *.cache
CLEAN_TARGET += *.data
CLEAN_TARGET += *.xpr
CLEAN_TARGET += xgui
CLEAN_TARGET +=  gui
CLEAN_TARGET += *.runs
CLEAN_TARGET += *.srcs
CLEAN_TARGET += *.sdk
CLEAN_TARGET += *.hw
CLEAN_TARGET += *.sim
CLEAN_TARGET += *.ip_user_files
CLEAN_TARGET += *.str
CLEAN_TARGET += mem_init_sys.txt
CLEAN_TARGET += *.csv
CLEAN_TARGET += *.hbs
CLEAN_TARGET += *.gen
CLEAN_TARGET += *.xpe
CLEAN_TARGET += *.xsa
CLEAN_TARGET += *.log
CLEAN_TARGET += *.jou
ifneq ($(strip $(DIR_NAME)), )
    CLEAN_TARGET := $(addprefix $(DIR_NAME)/,$(CLEAN_TARGET))
endif
CLEAN_TARGET += .Xil

CLEAN_DIRS := $(dir $(wildcard */*_vivado.log))

# Common dependencies that all projects have
M_DEPS += system_project.tcl
M_DEPS += system_bd.tcl
M_DEPS += $(wildcard system_top*.v)
M_DEPS += $(wildcard system_constr*.xdc) # Not all projects have this file
M_DEPS += $(wildcard system_constr*.tcl) # Not all projects have this file
M_DEPS += $(HDL_PROJECT_PATH)scripts/adi_project_xilinx.tcl
M_DEPS += $(HDL_PROJECT_PATH)../scripts/adi_env.tcl
M_DEPS += $(HDL_PROJECT_PATH)scripts/adi_board.tcl
M_DEPS += $(EXTERNAL_DEPS)

M_DEPS += $(foreach dep,$(LIB_DEPS),$(HDL_LIBRARY_PATH)$(dep)/component.xml)

.PHONY: all lib clean clean-all

all: external_dependencies $(PROJECT_NAME).sdk/system_top.xsa

lib: $(M_DEPS)

clean:
	-rm -f reference.dcp
	$(call clean, \
		$(CLEAN_TARGET), \
		$(HL)$(PROJECT_NAME)$(NC) project)
	-rm -Rf ${DIR_NAME}

clean-all: clean
	@rm -Rf $(CLEAN_DIRS)
	@for lib in $(LIB_DEPS); do \
		$(MAKE) -C $(HDL_LIBRARY_PATH)$${lib} clean; \
	done

external_dependencies: external_dependencies_cleanup $(EXTERNAL_DEPS)

external_dependencies_cleanup:
	rm -f missing_external.log

$(EXTERNAL_DEPS):
	if [ ! -d $@ ]; then \
		echo $@ >> missing_external.log ; \
	fi

MODE ?= "default"

$(PROJECT_NAME).sdk/system_top.xsa: $(M_DEPS)
	@if [ $(MODE) = incr ]; then \
		if [ -f */impl_1/system_top_routed.dcp ]; then \
			echo Found previous run result at `ls */impl_1/system_top_routed.dcp`; \
			cp -u */impl_1/system_top_routed.dcp ./reference.dcp ; \
		fi; \
		if [ -f ./reference.dcp ]; then \
			echo Using reference checkpoint for incremental compilation; \
		fi; \
	else \
		rm -f reference.dcp; \
	fi;
	$(call skip_if_missing, \
		Project, \
		$(PROJECT_NAME), \
		true, \
	rm -rf $(CLEAN_TARGET) ; \
	$(call build, \
		$(VIVADO) system_project.tcl, \
		$(PROJECT_NAME)_vivado.log, \
		$(HL)$(PROJECT_NAME)$(NC) project))

$(HDL_LIBRARY_PATH)%/component.xml: TARGET:=xilinx
FORCE:
$(HDL_LIBRARY_PATH)%/component.xml: FORCE
	flock $(dir $@).lock sh -c " \
	if [ -n \"${REQUIRED_VIVADO_VERSION}\" ]; then \
		$(MAKE) -C $(dir $@) $(TARGET) REQUIRED_VIVADO_VERSION=${REQUIRED_VIVADO_VERSION}; \
	else \
		$(MAKE) -C $(dir $@) $(TARGET); \
	fi"; exit $$?

===architecture.rst===
.. _architecture:

HDL Architecture
===============================================================================

Every HDL design of a reference project can be divided into:

#. Base design for the **carrier** board (projects/common/$CARRIER) ---
   description of what the carrier contains

   - an embedded processor - soft or hard;
   - all the peripheral IPs (that are necessary to run a Linux distribution
     on the system);
   - these designs are specific to each carrier, making them **carrier
     dependent**;
   - it describes part of the ``system_wrapper`` module;
   - located in :git-hdl:`projects/common`; one for each carrier;
   - here we do most of the PS configuration, add SPI, I2C and GPIOs;
   - in some cases, we have scripts to instantiate the PL DDR as ADC offload
     memory or DAC offload memory.

#. Base design for the **evaluation** board (projects/$EVAL_BOARD/common)
   --- description of what the evaluation contains

   - instantiates all the necessary IPs to control the evaluation board and to
     capture or send data;
   - the data paths defined in this block design are common across multiple
     carrier platforms, making them **carrier independent**;
   - it describes part of the ``system_wrapper`` module;
   - located at ``hdl/projects/$EVAL_BOARD/common`` (``*_bd.tcl`` for
     AMD Xilinx FPGAs, and ``*_qsys.tcl`` for Intel FPGAs).

#. Specific design for the system (projects/$EVAL_BOARD/$CARRIER)

   - we source the carrier board configuration (#1), then the evaluation
     board configuration (#2) and then we do some specific parameter
     modification, if required.

How they're instantiated
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In case of a project, inside the ``system_bd.tcl`` file we have to source
the base design of the carrier first (#1), then the base design of the
evaluation board (#2).

Example
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Take :adi:`FMCOMMS2 <AD-FMCOMMS2-EBZ>` with
:xilinx:`ZedBoard <products/boards-and-kits/1-8dyf-11.html>`;
the ``system_bd.tcl`` file will have the following designs sourced to be used:

.. code-block:: tcl

   source $ad_hdl_dir/projects/common/zed/zed_system_bd.tcl
   source ../common/fmcomms2_bd.tcl

Typical project diagram
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

.. image:: ./sources/base_platform.svg

Base Design
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The base design contains all the I/O peripherals, memory interfaces
and processing components, which are necessary for a fully functional
Linux system. The majority of these components are Intel and AMD Xilinx IP
cores.

Usually, they contain:

- Microprocessor
- Memory interface controller
- Peripheral interfaces

Microprocessor
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

In our designs, we use only three types:

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 2

   * - Intel
     -
     - AMD Xilinx
     -
     -
     - Lattice
   * - **SoC**
     - **FPGA**
     - **SoC**
     - **FPGA**
     - `ACAP`_
     - **FPGA**
   * - `HPS`_
     - `NIOS II`_
     - `PS7`_
       `PS8`_
     - `MicroBlaze`_
     - `Versal`_
     - `riscv-rx`_

.. _ACAP: https://www.xilinx.com/an/adaptive-compute-acceleration-platforms.html
.. _HPS: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/programmable/683458/current/hard-processor-system-hps.html
.. _NIOS II: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/products/programmable/processor/nios-ii.html
.. _PS7: https://www.xilinx.com/products/intellectual-property/processing_system7.html
.. _PS8: https://www.xilinx.com/products/intellectual-property/zynq-ultra-ps-e.html
.. _MicroBlaze: https://www.xilinx.com/products/design-tools/microblaze.html
.. _Versal: https://www.xilinx.com/products/silicon-devices/acap/versal.html
.. _riscv-rx: https://www.latticesemi.com/products/designsoftwareandip/intellectualproperty/ipcore/ipcores04/risc-v-rx-cpu

Worth mentioning in case of SoCs, the **Hard Processor System** (HPS)
or **Processing System 7/8** (PS7/8) do not contain just the dual-core
ARM® Cortex® - A9 MPCore™ processor, they also have other integrated
peripherals and memory interfaces. For more information please visit
the manufacturer's website, listed in the table above.

- ``PS7`` --- `Zynq-7000 SoC Processing
  System <https://docs.xilinx.com/v/u/en-US/pg082-processing-system7>`__
  (``processing_system7``)
- ``PS8`` --- `Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC Processing
  System <https://docs.xilinx.com/viewer/book-attachment/xFC3qkokxbD~75kj6nPLuw/2o4flzqn5OqWHaMHwpG3Qg>`__
  (``zynq_ultra_ps_e``)
- ``Versal`` --- `Versal ACAP
  CIPS <https://docs.xilinx.com/r/en-US/pg352-cips/Overview>`__
  (``versal_cips``)

Memory interface controller
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

In almost all cases, the carrier board is not made and designed by
:adi:`Analog Devices <>`, so the external memory solution of the system is
given.

Meaning, **we cannot support, modify or alter this important part** of the
system. In several cases we even have system limitations because of it
(e.g. the memory interface is not fast enough to handle the required
data throughput).

In the following two links, one can find the landing page of the available
memory solutions for Intel and AMD:

- Intel's memory interfaces:
  https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/programmable/support/support-resources/external-memory.html
- AMD's memory interfaces:
  https://www.xilinx.com/products/intellectual-property/mig.html#documentation

Peripheral interfaces
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

These interfaces are used to control external peripherals located on
the prototyping board or the FMC I/O board.

In HDL, these ports are named slightly different than how they're in
the documentations. Thus, to make it easier for beginners, here you
have the naming of the ports depending on the microprocessor used.

.. _architecture cpu-intercon-addr:

CPU/Memory interconnects addresses
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The memory addresses that will be used by software are based on the HDL
addresses of the IP register map, to which an offset is added, depending
on the architecture of the used FPGA (see also
:git-hdl:`ad_cpu_interconnect procedure <projects/scripts/adi_board.tcl>`;
architecture is specified by ``sys_zynq`` variable, for AMD FPGAs).

**Zynq-7000 and 7 Series**

Because this was the original target, this is the reference
address used, the common one, to which depending on the architecture,
you add an offset to get to the address space for the peripherals (as they
differ from one to the other).

**Zynq UltraScale+ MP**

If the address is between 0x4000_0000 - 0x4FFF_FFFF then the
AXI peripherics will be placed in 0x8000_0000 - 0x8FFF_FFFF range
by adding 0x4000_0000 to the address.

If the address is between 0x7000_0000 - 0x7FFF_FFFF then the
AXI peripherics will be placed in 0x9000_0000 - 0x9FFF_FFFF range
by adding 0x2000_0000 to the address.

**Versal**

If the address is between 0x4400_0000 - 0x4FFF_FFFF then the
AXI peripherics will be placed in 0xA400_0000 - 0xAFFF_FFFF range
by adding 0x6000_0000 to the address.

If the address is between 0x7000_0000 - 0x7FFF_FFFF then the
AXI peripherics will be placed in 0xB000_0000 - 0xBFFF_FFFF range
by adding 0x4000_0000 to the address.

**Intel**

Applying to DE10-Nano, C5SoC.

The address usually (but not always) starts from 0x0002_0000, or the first
available block of a bigger size. In Quartus block design you should be
able to determine it.

SPI
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

In general, the base design of the carrier (#1) has two Serial Peripheral
Interfaces (SPIs), which are used as a control interface for FMC/HSMC devices.
These SPI interfaces are controlled by the integrated SPI controller of the
**Hard Processor System** (HPS) or **Processing System 7/8** (PS7/8) or an
Intel or AMD SPI controller core.

I2C/I2S/SPDIF
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A couple of carriers require these standard interfaces for different purposes
(e.g. a configuration interface for an audio peripheral device).
These peripherals do not necessarily have vital roles in the reference
design -- it's more like a generic goal to support all the provided
peripherals of the carrier board.

HDMI
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

There is HDMI support for all carriers which are using the :adi:`ADV7511`
as HDMI transmitter. The HDMI transmitter core can be found
:git-hdl:`here (axi_hdmi_tx) <library/axi_hdmi_tx>`.

GPIOs
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The general rule of thumb is to define 64 GPIO pins for the design:

- bits [31: 0] always belong to the carrier board;
- bits [63:32] will be assigned to switches, buttons and/or LEDs, which
  can be found on the FMC board;
- bits [95:64] will be used when the FPGA type is Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC.

When some of these GPIOs are not used, the input pins should have the
output pins driven to them, so that
:xilinx:`Vivado <products/design-tools/vivado.html>` will not complain about
inputs not being assigned to.

Depending on the processor type, add these values to the GPIO number
from the HDL project to obtain the final number used in software:

- PS7 EMIO offset = **54**
- PS8 EMIO offset = **78**
- MicroBlaze offset = **no offset**
- Versal offset = **-32**

Connectivity
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

- Ethernet
- USB OTG

These interface designs are borrowed from the golden reference design
of the board.

Interrupts
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

When developing the Linux software parts for an HDL project, the
interrupts number to the PS have a different number in the software
side.

Not a rule, but in our designs we preffer to use firstly the interrupts
from 15 and to go down to 0. Be careful when assigning one, because it
might be used in the base design of the carrier!

Always check which are used (in
``/projects/common/$carrier/$carrier_system_bd.tcl``)

Memory Specifications
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This section documents the on-chip and external memory resources of each
supported carrier.

.. important::

   **This section is a work in progress.**

   - Data was pulled from a large number of user guides, device datasheets,
     and technical reference manuals. **Mistakes or gaps are possible**.
   - Memory configurations **can vary between board revisions** so what is
     listed here may not match your specific revision.

   Always cross-reference with the official documentation for your board
   before making any design decisions based on these numbers.

On-Chip Memory
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

- **BRAM** and **UltraRAM** reside in the programmable logic fabric and are
  fully available to HDL designs.
- **UltraRAM** (288 Kb blocks) is present only on UltraScale+ and Versal
  devices.
- Lattice CertusPro-NX provides **EBR** (18 Kb) and **LRAM** (512 Kb) blocks.
- Intel Arria 10 / Stratix 10 / Agilex 7 use **M20K** (20 Kb) blocks while
  Cyclone V uses **M10K** (10 Kb) blocks.
- The **PS/HPS OCM SRAM** is a fixed block inside the processor subsystem
  (Zynq-7000, Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC, Versal) shared between the
  APU/application processors and PL via the OCM interconnect. Cyclone V
  and Agilex 7 HPS include a smaller 64 KB or 256 KB OCRAM used by the
  preloader before DDR initialisation.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~


  - **PS-side / HPS-side** memory is connected to the hard processor system

  - **PL-side / Fabric-side** memory is connected directly to FPGA fabric
    I/O banks and is available for HDL data-path designs.
  - On **Versal** devices there is no hard PS/PL split; all DDR interfaces
    connect via the Network on Chip (NoC).

.. note::

   ``Rate (MT/s) x (effective data width in bytes)``.

   error-correction overhead, not user payload.

   not 2,666 x 9 = ~24.0 GB/s.

1	===architecture.rst===
2	.. _architecture:
3	
4	HDL Architecture
5	===============================================================================
6	
7	Every HDL design of a reference project can be divided into:
8	
9	#. Base design for the **carrier** board (projects/common/$CARRIER) ---
10	   description of what the carrier contains
11	
12	   - an embedded processor - soft or hard;
13	   - all the peripheral IPs (that are necessary to run a Linux distribution
14	     on the system);
15	   - these designs are specific to each carrier, making them **carrier
16	     dependent**;
17	   - it describes part of the ``system_wrapper`` module;
18	   - located in :git-hdl:`projects/common`; one for each carrier;
19	   - here we do most of the PS configuration, add SPI, I2C and GPIOs;
20	   - in some cases, we have scripts to instantiate the PL DDR as ADC offload
21	     memory or DAC offload memory.
22	
23	#. Base design for the **evaluation** board (projects/$EVAL_BOARD/common)
24	   --- description of what the evaluation contains
25	
26	   - instantiates all the necessary IPs to control the evaluation board and to
27	     capture or send data;
28	   - the data paths defined in this block design are common across multiple
29	     carrier platforms, making them **carrier independent**;
30	   - it describes part of the ``system_wrapper`` module;
31	   - located at ``hdl/projects/$EVAL_BOARD/common`` (``*_bd.tcl`` for
32	     AMD Xilinx FPGAs, and ``*_qsys.tcl`` for Intel FPGAs).
33	
34	#. Specific design for the system (projects/$EVAL_BOARD/$CARRIER)
35	
36	   - we source the carrier board configuration (#1), then the evaluation
37	     board configuration (#2) and then we do some specific parameter
38	     modification, if required.
39	
40	How they're instantiated
41	-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
42	
43	In case of a project, inside the ``system_bd.tcl`` file we have to source
44	the base design of the carrier first (#1), then the base design of the
45	evaluation board (#2).
46	
47	Example
48	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
49	
50	Take :adi:`FMCOMMS2 <AD-FMCOMMS2-EBZ>` with
51	:xilinx:`ZedBoard <products/boards-and-kits/1-8dyf-11.html>`;
52	the ``system_bd.tcl`` file will have the following designs sourced to be used:
53	
54	.. code-block:: tcl
55	
56	   source $ad_hdl_dir/projects/common/zed/zed_system_bd.tcl
57	   source ../common/fmcomms2_bd.tcl
58	
59	Typical project diagram
60	-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
61	
62	.. image:: ./sources/base_platform.svg
63	
64	Base Design
65	-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
66	
67	The base design contains all the I/O peripherals, memory interfaces
68	and processing components, which are necessary for a fully functional
69	Linux system. The majority of these components are Intel and AMD Xilinx IP
70	cores.
71	
72	Usually, they contain:
73	
74	- Microprocessor
75	- Memory interface controller
76	- Peripheral interfaces
77	
78	Microprocessor
79	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
80	
81	In our designs, we use only three types:
82	
83	.. list-table::
84	   :header-rows: 2
85	
86	   * - Intel
87	     -
88	     - AMD Xilinx
89	     -
90	     -
91	     - Lattice
92	   * - **SoC**
93	     - **FPGA**
94	     - **SoC**
95	     - **FPGA**
96	     - `ACAP`_
97	     - **FPGA**
98	   * - `HPS`_
99	     - `NIOS II`_
100	     - `PS7`_
101	       `PS8`_
102	     - `MicroBlaze`_
103	     - `Versal`_
104	     - `riscv-rx`_
105	
106	.. _ACAP: https://www.xilinx.com/an/adaptive-compute-acceleration-platforms.html
107	.. _HPS: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/programmable/683458/current/hard-processor-system-hps.html
108	.. _NIOS II: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/products/programmable/processor/nios-ii.html
109	.. _PS7: https://www.xilinx.com/products/intellectual-property/processing_system7.html
110	.. _PS8: https://www.xilinx.com/products/intellectual-property/zynq-ultra-ps-e.html
111	.. _MicroBlaze: https://www.xilinx.com/products/design-tools/microblaze.html
112	.. _Versal: https://www.xilinx.com/products/silicon-devices/acap/versal.html
113	.. _riscv-rx: https://www.latticesemi.com/products/designsoftwareandip/intellectualproperty/ipcore/ipcores04/risc-v-rx-cpu
114	
115	Worth mentioning in case of SoCs, the **Hard Processor System** (HPS)
116	or **Processing System 7/8** (PS7/8) do not contain just the dual-core
117	ARM® Cortex® - A9 MPCore™ processor, they also have other integrated
118	peripherals and memory interfaces. For more information please visit
119	the manufacturer's website, listed in the table above.
120	
121	- ``PS7`` --- `Zynq-7000 SoC Processing
122	  System <https://docs.xilinx.com/v/u/en-US/pg082-processing-system7>`__
123	  (``processing_system7``)
124	- ``PS8`` --- `Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC Processing
125	  System <https://docs.xilinx.com/viewer/book-attachment/xFC3qkokxbD~75kj6nPLuw/2o4flzqn5OqWHaMHwpG3Qg>`__
126	  (``zynq_ultra_ps_e``)
127	- ``Versal`` --- `Versal ACAP
128	  CIPS <https://docs.xilinx.com/r/en-US/pg352-cips/Overview>`__
129	  (``versal_cips``)
130	
131	Memory interface controller
132	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
133	
134	In almost all cases, the carrier board is not made and designed by
135	:adi:`Analog Devices <>`, so the external memory solution of the system is
136	given.
137	
138	Meaning, **we cannot support, modify or alter this important part** of the
139	system. In several cases we even have system limitations because of it
140	(e.g. the memory interface is not fast enough to handle the required
141	data throughput).
142	
143	In the following two links, one can find the landing page of the available
144	memory solutions for Intel and AMD:
145	
146	- Intel's memory interfaces:
147	  https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/programmable/support/support-resources/external-memory.html
148	- AMD's memory interfaces:
149	  https://www.xilinx.com/products/intellectual-property/mig.html#documentation
150	
151	Peripheral interfaces
152	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
153	
154	These interfaces are used to control external peripherals located on
155	the prototyping board or the FMC I/O board.
156	
157	In HDL, these ports are named slightly different than how they're in
158	the documentations. Thus, to make it easier for beginners, here you
159	have the naming of the ports depending on the microprocessor used.
160	
161	.. _architecture cpu-intercon-addr:
162	
163	CPU/Memory interconnects addresses
164	^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
165	
166	The memory addresses that will be used by software are based on the HDL
167	addresses of the IP register map, to which an offset is added, depending
168	on the architecture of the used FPGA (see also
169	:git-hdl:`ad_cpu_interconnect procedure <projects/scripts/adi_board.tcl>`;
170	architecture is specified by ``sys_zynq`` variable, for AMD FPGAs).
171	
172	**Zynq-7000 and 7 Series**
173	
174	Because this was the original target, this is the reference
175	address used, the common one, to which depending on the architecture,
176	you add an offset to get to the address space for the peripherals (as they
177	differ from one to the other).
178	
179	**Zynq UltraScale+ MP**
180	
181	If the address is between 0x4000_0000 - 0x4FFF_FFFF then the
182	AXI peripherics will be placed in 0x8000_0000 - 0x8FFF_FFFF range
183	by adding 0x4000_0000 to the address.
184	
185	If the address is between 0x7000_0000 - 0x7FFF_FFFF then the
186	AXI peripherics will be placed in 0x9000_0000 - 0x9FFF_FFFF range
187	by adding 0x2000_0000 to the address.
188	
189	**Versal**
190	
191	If the address is between 0x4400_0000 - 0x4FFF_FFFF then the
192	AXI peripherics will be placed in 0xA400_0000 - 0xAFFF_FFFF range
193	by adding 0x6000_0000 to the address.
194	
195	If the address is between 0x7000_0000 - 0x7FFF_FFFF then the
196	AXI peripherics will be placed in 0xB000_0000 - 0xBFFF_FFFF range
197	by adding 0x4000_0000 to the address.
198	
199	**Intel**
200	
201	Applying to DE10-Nano, C5SoC.
202	
203	The address usually (but not always) starts from 0x0002_0000, or the first
204	available block of a bigger size. In Quartus block design you should be
205	able to determine it.
206	
207	SPI
208	^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
209	
210	In general, the base design of the carrier (#1) has two Serial Peripheral
211	Interfaces (SPIs), which are used as a control interface for FMC/HSMC devices.
212	These SPI interfaces are controlled by the integrated SPI controller of the
213	**Hard Processor System** (HPS) or **Processing System 7/8** (PS7/8) or an
214	Intel or AMD SPI controller core.
215	
216	I2C/I2S/SPDIF
217	^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
218	
219	A couple of carriers require these standard interfaces for different purposes
220	(e.g. a configuration interface for an audio peripheral device).
221	These peripherals do not necessarily have vital roles in the reference
222	design -- it's more like a generic goal to support all the provided
223	peripherals of the carrier board.
224	
225	HDMI
226	^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
227	
228	There is HDMI support for all carriers which are using the :adi:`ADV7511`
229	as HDMI transmitter. The HDMI transmitter core can be found
230	:git-hdl:`here (axi_hdmi_tx) <library/axi_hdmi_tx>`.
231	
232	GPIOs
233	^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
234	
235	The general rule of thumb is to define 64 GPIO pins for the design:
236	
237	- bits [31: 0] always belong to the carrier board;
238	- bits [63:32] will be assigned to switches, buttons and/or LEDs, which
239	  can be found on the FMC board;
240	- bits [95:64] will be used when the FPGA type is Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC.
241	
242	When some of these GPIOs are not used, the input pins should have the
243	output pins driven to them, so that
244	:xilinx:`Vivado <products/design-tools/vivado.html>` will not complain about
245	inputs not being assigned to.
246	
247	Depending on the processor type, add these values to the GPIO number
248	from the HDL project to obtain the final number used in software:
249	
250	- PS7 EMIO offset = **54**
251	- PS8 EMIO offset = **78**
252	- MicroBlaze offset = **no offset**
253	- Versal offset = **-32**
254	
255	Connectivity
256	^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
257	
258	- Ethernet
259	- USB OTG
260	
261	These interface designs are borrowed from the golden reference design
262	of the board.
263	
264	Interrupts
265	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
266	
267	When developing the Linux software parts for an HDL project, the
268	interrupts number to the PS have a different number in the software
269	side.
270	
271	Not a rule, but in our designs we preffer to use firstly the interrupts
272	from 15 and to go down to 0. Be careful when assigning one, because it
273	might be used in the base design of the carrier!
274	
275	Always check which are used (in
276	``/projects/common/$carrier/$carrier_system_bd.tcl``)
277

548	Memory Specifications
549	-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
550	
551	This section documents the on-chip and external memory resources of each
552	supported carrier.
553	
554	.. important::
555	
556	   **This section is a work in progress.**
557	
558	   - Data was pulled from a large number of user guides, device datasheets,
559	     and technical reference manuals. **Mistakes or gaps are possible**.
560	   - Memory configurations **can vary between board revisions** so what is
561	     listed here may not match your specific revision.
562	
563	   Always cross-reference with the official documentation for your board
564	   before making any design decisions based on these numbers.
565	
566	On-Chip Memory
567	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
568	
569	- **BRAM** and **UltraRAM** reside in the programmable logic fabric and are
570	  fully available to HDL designs.
571	- **UltraRAM** (288 Kb blocks) is present only on UltraScale+ and Versal
572	  devices.
573	- Lattice CertusPro-NX provides **EBR** (18 Kb) and **LRAM** (512 Kb) blocks.
574	- Intel Arria 10 / Stratix 10 / Agilex 7 use **M20K** (20 Kb) blocks while
575	  Cyclone V uses **M10K** (10 Kb) blocks.
576	- The **PS/HPS OCM SRAM** is a fixed block inside the processor subsystem
577	  (Zynq-7000, Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC, Versal) shared between the
578	  APU/application processors and PL via the OCM interconnect. Cyclone V
579	  and Agilex 7 HPS include a smaller 64 KB or 256 KB OCRAM used by the
580	  preloader before DDR initialisation.

740	External Memory
741	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
742	
743	
744	  - **PS-side / HPS-side** memory is connected to the hard processor system
745	    and is the primary DRAM for Linux.
746	  - **PL-side / Fabric-side** memory is connected directly to FPGA fabric
747	    I/O banks and is available for HDL data-path designs.
748	  - On **Versal** devices there is no hard PS/PL split; all DDR interfaces
749	    connect via the Network on Chip (NoC).
750	
751	.. note::
752	
753	   **Bandwidth** figures in the tables below are computed as
754	   ``Rate (MT/s) x (effective data width in bytes)``.
755	   On 72-bit ECC interfaces (64-bit data + 8-bit ECC), only the
756	   64-bit / 8-byte data portion is counted - the ECC byte carries
757	   error-correction overhead, not user payload.
758	   Example: a 72-bit DDR4-2666 interface => 2,666 x 8 = ~21.3 GB/s,
759	   not 2,666 x 9 = ~24.0 GB/s.

===architecture.rst===
.. _architecture:

HDL Architecture
===============================================================================

Every HDL design of a reference project can be divided into:

#. Base design for the **carrier** board (projects/common/$CARRIER) ---
   description of what the carrier contains

   - an embedded processor - soft or hard;
   - all the peripheral IPs (that are necessary to run a Linux distribution
     on the system);
   - these designs are specific to each carrier, making them **carrier
     dependent**;
   - it describes part of the ``system_wrapper`` module;
   - located in :git-hdl:`projects/common`; one for each carrier;
   - here we do most of the PS configuration, add SPI, I2C and GPIOs;
   - in some cases, we have scripts to instantiate the PL DDR as ADC offload
     memory or DAC offload memory.

#. Base design for the **evaluation** board (projects/$EVAL_BOARD/common)
   --- description of what the evaluation contains

   - instantiates all the necessary IPs to control the evaluation board and to
     capture or send data;
   - the data paths defined in this block design are common across multiple
     carrier platforms, making them **carrier independent**;
   - it describes part of the ``system_wrapper`` module;
   - located at ``hdl/projects/$EVAL_BOARD/common`` (``*_bd.tcl`` for
     AMD Xilinx FPGAs, and ``*_qsys.tcl`` for Intel FPGAs).

#. Specific design for the system (projects/$EVAL_BOARD/$CARRIER)

   - we source the carrier board configuration (#1), then the evaluation
     board configuration (#2) and then we do some specific parameter
     modification, if required.

How they're instantiated
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In case of a project, inside the ``system_bd.tcl`` file we have to source
the base design of the carrier first (#1), then the base design of the
evaluation board (#2).

Example
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Take :adi:`FMCOMMS2 <AD-FMCOMMS2-EBZ>` with
:xilinx:`ZedBoard <products/boards-and-kits/1-8dyf-11.html>`;
the ``system_bd.tcl`` file will have the following designs sourced to be used:

.. code-block:: tcl

   source $ad_hdl_dir/projects/common/zed/zed_system_bd.tcl
   source ../common/fmcomms2_bd.tcl

Typical project diagram
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

.. image:: ./sources/base_platform.svg

Base Design
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The base design contains all the I/O peripherals, memory interfaces
and processing components, which are necessary for a fully functional
Linux system. The majority of these components are Intel and AMD Xilinx IP
cores.

Usually, they contain:

- Microprocessor
- Memory interface controller
- Peripheral interfaces

Microprocessor
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

In our designs, we use only three types:

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 2

   * - Intel
     -
     - AMD Xilinx
     -
     -
     - Lattice
   * - **SoC**
     - **FPGA**
     - **SoC**
     - **FPGA**
     - `ACAP`_
     - **FPGA**
   * - `HPS`_
     - `NIOS II`_
     - `PS7`_
       `PS8`_
     - `MicroBlaze`_
     - `Versal`_
     - `riscv-rx`_

.. _ACAP: https://www.xilinx.com/an/adaptive-compute-acceleration-platforms.html
.. _HPS: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/programmable/683458/current/hard-processor-system-hps.html
.. _NIOS II: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/products/programmable/processor/nios-ii.html
.. _PS7: https://www.xilinx.com/products/intellectual-property/processing_system7.html
.. _PS8: https://www.xilinx.com/products/intellectual-property/zynq-ultra-ps-e.html
.. _MicroBlaze: https://www.xilinx.com/products/design-tools/microblaze.html
.. _Versal: https://www.xilinx.com/products/silicon-devices/acap/versal.html
.. _riscv-rx: https://www.latticesemi.com/products/designsoftwareandip/intellectualproperty/ipcore/ipcores04/risc-v-rx-cpu

Worth mentioning in case of SoCs, the **Hard Processor System** (HPS)
or **Processing System 7/8** (PS7/8) do not contain just the dual-core
ARM® Cortex® - A9 MPCore™ processor, they also have other integrated
peripherals and memory interfaces. For more information please visit
the manufacturer's website, listed in the table above.

- ``PS7`` --- `Zynq-7000 SoC Processing
  System <https://docs.xilinx.com/v/u/en-US/pg082-processing-system7>`__
  (``processing_system7``)
- ``PS8`` --- `Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC Processing
  System <https://docs.xilinx.com/viewer/book-attachment/xFC3qkokxbD~75kj6nPLuw/2o4flzqn5OqWHaMHwpG3Qg>`__
  (``zynq_ultra_ps_e``)
- ``Versal`` --- `Versal ACAP
  CIPS <https://docs.xilinx.com/r/en-US/pg352-cips/Overview>`__
  (``versal_cips``)

Memory interface controller
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

In almost all cases, the carrier board is not made and designed by
:adi:`Analog Devices <>`, so the external memory solution of the system is
given.

Meaning, **we cannot support, modify or alter this important part** of the
system. In several cases we even have system limitations because of it
(e.g. the memory interface is not fast enough to handle the required
data throughput).

In the following two links, one can find the landing page of the available
memory solutions for Intel and AMD:

- Intel's memory interfaces:
  https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/programmable/support/support-resources/external-memory.html
- AMD's memory interfaces:
  https://www.xilinx.com/products/intellectual-property/mig.html#documentation

Peripheral interfaces
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

These interfaces are used to control external peripherals located on
the prototyping board or the FMC I/O board.

In HDL, these ports are named slightly different than how they're in
the documentations. Thus, to make it easier for beginners, here you
have the naming of the ports depending on the microprocessor used.

.. _architecture cpu-intercon-addr:

CPU/Memory interconnects addresses
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The memory addresses that will be used by software are based on the HDL
addresses of the IP register map, to which an offset is added, depending
on the architecture of the used FPGA (see also
:git-hdl:`ad_cpu_interconnect procedure <projects/scripts/adi_board.tcl>`;
architecture is specified by ``sys_zynq`` variable, for AMD FPGAs).

**Zynq-7000 and 7 Series**

Because this was the original target, this is the reference
address used, the common one, to which depending on the architecture,
you add an offset to get to the address space for the peripherals (as they
differ from one to the other).

**Zynq UltraScale+ MP**

If the address is between 0x4000_0000 - 0x4FFF_FFFF then the
AXI peripherics will be placed in 0x8000_0000 - 0x8FFF_FFFF range
by adding 0x4000_0000 to the address.

If the address is between 0x7000_0000 - 0x7FFF_FFFF then the
AXI peripherics will be placed in 0x9000_0000 - 0x9FFF_FFFF range
by adding 0x2000_0000 to the address.

**Versal**

If the address is between 0x4400_0000 - 0x4FFF_FFFF then the
AXI peripherics will be placed in 0xA400_0000 - 0xAFFF_FFFF range
by adding 0x6000_0000 to the address.

If the address is between 0x7000_0000 - 0x7FFF_FFFF then the
AXI peripherics will be placed in 0xB000_0000 - 0xBFFF_FFFF range
by adding 0x4000_0000 to the address.

**Intel**

Applying to DE10-Nano, C5SoC.

The address usually (but not always) starts from 0x0002_0000, or the first
available block of a bigger size. In Quartus block design you should be
able to determine it.

SPI
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

In general, the base design of the carrier (#1) has two Serial Peripheral
Interfaces (SPIs), which are used as a control interface for FMC/HSMC devices.
These SPI interfaces are controlled by the integrated SPI controller of the
**Hard Processor System** (HPS) or **Processing System 7/8** (PS7/8) or an
Intel or AMD SPI controller core.

I2C/I2S/SPDIF
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A couple of carriers require these standard interfaces for different purposes
(e.g. a configuration interface for an audio peripheral device).
These peripherals do not necessarily have vital roles in the reference
design -- it's more like a generic goal to support all the provided
peripherals of the carrier board.

HDMI
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

There is HDMI support for all carriers which are using the :adi:`ADV7511`
as HDMI transmitter. The HDMI transmitter core can be found
:git-hdl:`here (axi_hdmi_tx) <library/axi_hdmi_tx>`.

GPIOs
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The general rule of thumb is to define 64 GPIO pins for the design:

- bits [31: 0] always belong to the carrier board;
- bits [63:32] will be assigned to switches, buttons and/or LEDs, which
  can be found on the FMC board;
- bits [95:64] will be used when the FPGA type is Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC.

When some of these GPIOs are not used, the input pins should have the
output pins driven to them, so that
:xilinx:`Vivado <products/design-tools/vivado.html>` will not complain about
inputs not being assigned to.

Depending on the processor type, add these values to the GPIO number
from the HDL project to obtain the final number used in software:

- PS7 EMIO offset = **54**
- PS8 EMIO offset = **78**
- MicroBlaze offset = **no offset**
- Versal offset = **-32**

Connectivity
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

- Ethernet
- USB OTG

These interface designs are borrowed from the golden reference design
of the board.

Interrupts
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

When developing the Linux software parts for an HDL project, the
interrupts number to the PS have a different number in the software
side.

Not a rule, but in our designs we preffer to use firstly the interrupts
from 15 and to go down to 0. Be careful when assigning one, because it
might be used in the base design of the carrier!

Always check which are used (in
``/projects/common/$carrier/$carrier_system_bd.tcl``)

Memory Specifications
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This section documents the on-chip and external memory resources of each
supported carrier.

.. important::

   **This section is a work in progress.**

   - Data was pulled from a large number of user guides, device datasheets,
     and technical reference manuals. **Mistakes or gaps are possible**.
   - Memory configurations **can vary between board revisions** so what is
     listed here may not match your specific revision.

   Always cross-reference with the official documentation for your board
   before making any design decisions based on these numbers.

On-Chip Memory
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

- **BRAM** and **UltraRAM** reside in the programmable logic fabric and are
  fully available to HDL designs.
- **UltraRAM** (288 Kb blocks) is present only on UltraScale+ and Versal
  devices.
- Lattice CertusPro-NX provides **EBR** (18 Kb) and **LRAM** (512 Kb) blocks.
- Intel Arria 10 / Stratix 10 / Agilex 7 use **M20K** (20 Kb) blocks while
  Cyclone V uses **M10K** (10 Kb) blocks.
- The **PS/HPS OCM SRAM** is a fixed block inside the processor subsystem
  (Zynq-7000, Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC, Versal) shared between the
  APU/application processors and PL via the OCM interconnect. Cyclone V
  and Agilex 7 HPS include a smaller 64 KB or 256 KB OCRAM used by the
  preloader before DDR initialisation.

External Memory
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~


  - **PS-side / HPS-side** memory is connected to the hard processor system
    and is the primary DRAM for Linux.
  - **PL-side / Fabric-side** memory is connected directly to FPGA fabric
    I/O banks and is available for HDL data-path designs.
  - On **Versal** devices there is no hard PS/PL split; all DDR interfaces
    connect via the Network on Chip (NoC).

.. note::

   **Bandwidth** figures in the tables below are computed as
   ``Rate (MT/s) x (effective data width in bytes)``.
   On 72-bit ECC interfaces (64-bit data + 8-bit ECC), only the
   64-bit / 8-byte data portion is counted - the ECC byte carries
   error-correction overhead, not user payload.
   Example: a 72-bit DDR4-2666 interface => 2,666 x 8 = ~21.3 GB/s,
   not 2,666 x 9 = ~24.0 GB/s.

        the **HPS DDR4 HiLo card (J13) is not included** with the H-Tile kit
        and must be purchased separately.
      - :intel:`FM87 <content/www/us/en/products/details/fpga/development-kits/agilex/si-agi027.html>`:
        **DIMM2 (J5) is unpopulated** at the factory - socket only, available
        on the AGF027 variant only.

File structure of a project
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

.. tip::

   In ``/projects/common/$carrier_name/`` you can find templates for the
   *system_top.v*, *Makefile*, etc. to help you when creating a new project.

Project files for AMD boards
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

A project for an AMD FPGA board should contain the following files:

- ``Makefile`` --- auto-generated file; contains all the IP
  dependencies needed for the project to be built
- ``system_project.tcl`` --- script that creates the actual Vivado
  project and runs the synthesis/implementation of the design
- ``system_bd.tcl`` --- sources the base design of the carrier first, then the
  base design of the evaluation board, and afterwards it contains all the IP
  instances and connections that must be added on top of the sourced files, to
  complete the design of the project (these are **specific** to the
  combination of this carrier and board)
- ``system_constr.xdc`` --- constraints file of the design; it's the
  connection between the physical pins of the FPGA and the HDL code
  that describes the behavior; here you define the FMC I/O pins,
  board-specific clock signals, timing constraints, etc. The
  constraints specific to the carrier are imported in the
  *system_project.tcl* file
- ``system_top.v`` --- contains everything about the HDL part of the
  project; it instantiates the ``system_wrapper`` module, I/O buffers,
  I/ODDRs, modules that transform signals from LVDS to single-ended,
  etc. The I/O ports of this Verilog module will be connected to actual
  I/O pads of the FPGA.

  - ``system_wrapper`` --- is a tool-generated file and can be found at
    ``<project_name>.srcs/sources_1/bd/system/hdl/system_wrapper.v``

    - the I/O ports of this module are declared in either
      *system_bd.tcl* or in the base design of the evaluation board (#2) file
    - this can be visualized in Vivado at the Block Design section
    - the base design, board design and system_bd.tcl describe this
      module, making the connections between the instantiated IPs

Project files for Intel boards
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

A project for an Intel FPGA board should contain the following files:

- ``Makefile`` --- auto-generated file; contains all the IP
  dependencies needed for the project to be built
- ``system_project.tcl`` --- script that creates the actual Quartus
  project and runs the synthesis/implementation of the design. It also
  contains the I/O definitions for the interfaces between the board and
  the FPGA
- ``system_qsys.tcl`` --- also called **platform designer**; sources the base
  design of the carrier first, then the base design of the evaluation board,
  and afterwards it contains all the IP instances and connections that must
  be added on top of the sourced files, to complete the design of the project
  (these are specific to the combination of this carrier and board)
- ``system_constr.sdc`` --- contains clock definitions and other path
  constraints
- ``system_top.v`` --- contains everything about the HDL part of the
  project; it instantiates the ``system_bd`` module, I/O buffers, specific
  SPI modules, modules that transform signals from LVDS to single-ended,
  etc. The I/O ports of this Verilog module will be connected to actual
  I/O pads of the FPGA

Examples
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Some carriers have a different name for these files, for example A10SoC
has constraints file for both PL side and PS side:

- a10soc_plddr4_assign.tcl --- constraints file for the PL
- a10soc_system_assign.tcl --- constraints file for the PS

Project files for Lattice boards
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

A project for a Lattice FPGA board should contain the following files:

- ``Makefile`` --- auto-generated file; contains all the IP
  dependencies needed for the project to be built
- ``system_project_pb.tcl`` --- used to build the Propel Builder project
  (block design); linked in project-lattice.mk, run by propelbld (Windows),
  propelbldwrap (Linux);
- ``system_project.tcl`` --- used to build the Radiant project; Linked in
  project-lattice.mk, run by pnmainc (Windows), radiantc (Linux);
- ``system_pb.tcl`` --- linker script for the projects, sourced in
  adi_project_pb procedure that is called in system_project_pb.tcl and it is
  defined in adi_project_lattice_pb.tcl; sources the base design of the carrier
  first, then the base design of the evaluation board, and afterwards it
  contains all the IP instances and connections that must be added on top of
  the sourced files, to complete the design of the project (these are specific
  to the combination of this carrier and board)
- ``system_constr.sdc`` --- contains clock definitions and other path constraints
- ``system_constr.pdc`` --- contains clock definitions and other path
  constraints  + physical constraints
- ``system_top.v`` --- contains everything about the HDL part of the
  project; it instantiates the **<project_name>.v** ``system_wrapper`` module,
  I/O buffers, I/ODDRs, modules that transform signals from LVDS to single-ended,
  etc. The I/O ports of this Verilog module will be connected to actual
  I/O pads of the FPGA

I now have a very comprehensive understanding of this project. Let me summarize what I've learned:

## Project: analogdevicesinc/hdl
**What it is:** A collection of HDL (Verilog/VHDL) reference designs and IP libraries for Analog Devices FPGA-based prototyping/reference systems. It builds FPGA designs for AMD Xilinx, Intel, and Lattice toolchains.

## Key structure:
1. **library/** — ~97 IP core modules (reusable HDL blocks), organized by vendor
   - `axi_*` — AXI IP cores (ADC/DAC interfaces, data converters like axi_ad9361, axi_dmac, etc.)
   - `util_*` — utility IPs (FIFOs, CDC, pack/unpack, filters)
   - `common/` — shared Verilog utilities (ad_iobuf, up_axi, ad_mem, etc.)
   - `spi_engine/` — SPI engine framework
   - `jesd204/` — JESD204B/C framework
   - `interfaces/` — interface definitions
2. **projects/** — ~99 reference designs, each is a carrier+eval-board combo
   - `projects/common/$CARRIER/` — carrier base designs (carrier-dependent)
   - `projects/$EVAL/common/` — eval board base design (carrier-independent)
   - `projects/$EVAL/$CARRIER/` — specific design combination
3. **projects/scripts/** — build machinery (Tcl procs + Makefiles)
   - `adi_project_xilinx.tcl`, `adi_project_intel.tcl`, `adi_project_lattice.tcl`
   - `adi_board.tcl` — board helpers (ad_cpu_interconnect, ad_connect, etc.)
   - `project-xilinx.mk`, `project-intel.mk`, `project-lattice.mk`
   - `adi_env.tcl` (root scripts/) — environment/version setup
4. **library/scripts/** — library build machinery
   - `library.mk`, `adi_ip_xilinx.tcl`, `adi_ip_intel.tcl`, `adi_ip_lattice.tcl`
5. **docs/** — Sphinx documentation
   - user_guide/ (architecture, build_hdl, customize_hdl, porting_project, hdl_coding_guidelines, releases)
   - library/ (per-IP docs)
   - regmap/ (register map text files)

## Project file structure (per project):
- `Makefile` (auto-generated, IP deps)
- `system_project.tcl` (creates Vivado project, runs synth/impl)
- `system_bd.tcl` (sources carrier + eval base designs, adds IP instances)
- `system_constr.xdc` (pin constraints)
- `system_top.v` (top module, instantiates system_wrapper + IO buffers)

## Library module structure:
- `Makefile` with GENERIC_DEPS, XILINX_DEPS, INTEL_DEPS, LATTICE_DEPS
- `*_ip.tcl` (Xilinx IP packaging), `*_hw.tcl` (Intel), `*_ltt.tcl` (Lattice)
- `*_regmap.v` (register maps)
- `bd/bd.tcl` (block design)
- `tb/` (testbenches)

## Key mechanisms:
- **up_axi.v** — AXI-lite to internal register interface (microprocessor interface)
- **ad_cpu_interconnect** — connects AXI peripherals to CPU
- **ad_connect** — connects block design nets
- **adi_env.tcl** — version checking (Vivado 2025.1, Quartus 25.3, Lattice 2025.2)
- **regmap txt files** — register map definitions (docs/regmap)

## Build flow:
1. `make` in project dir → project-xilinx.mk
2. Builds library deps (component.xml) via flock'd parallel make
3. Runs `vivado -source system_project.tcl`
4. system_project.tcl calls adi_project → adi_project_create → adi_project_files → adi_project_run

## Multi-vendor support:
- AMD Xilinx (Vivado) — primary
- Intel (Quartus) — qsys/platform designer
- Lattice (Radiant/Propel)

input.rationale: 本仓库是 Analog Devices 的 FPGA HDL 参考设计库，体量庞大（约 97 个 library IP 模块、约 99 个 projects 参考设计，并支持 AMD Xilinx / Intel / Lattice 三家工具链）。学习路线按"先看清全貌、再拆构建系统、再读 IP 库与数据通路、最后做扩展与移植"的认知顺序设计为 8 个单元 28 篇讲义。第 1、2 单元（beginner）解决"它是什么、目录怎么组织、怎么把它跑起来、单工程由哪些文件构成"这一从零起步问题；第 3、4 单元（intermediate）拆解贯穿全仓的两套核心机制——基于 GNU Make + Tcl 的工程/库构建流水线（projects/scripts 与 library/scripts）以及多厂商 IP 打包与寄存器映射（up_axi）；第 5、6 单元（intermediate）深入数据通路（axi_dmac、数据转换器 IP、util 工具 IP）与两大框架（JESD204、SPI Engine）；第 7、8 单元（advanced）面向二次开发与质量保障，覆盖移植、新建工程、多厂商构建、仿真测试、编码规范、收发器与时序、Boot 镜像与发布。讲义之间用 depends_on 显式织成依赖链，确保读者总能按拓扑顺序逐篇推进；每篇均只讲一个独立主题，并给出基于真实源码的可操作实践任务。

lectures.title: ADI HDL 项目总览：它是什么、为谁服务
lectures.topic: 介绍 Analog Devices HDL 参考设计库的整体定位：用 Verilog/VHDL 与 Tcl 脚本为各类 ADI 评估板生成可在 AMD Xilinx、Intel、Lattice FPGA 上综合的参考设计。
learning_goals: 理解仓库提供的是参考设计与可复用 IP 库，而非单一应用
区分 library（IP 库）与 projects（参考设计）两大组成部分
了解 ADI HDL 与 no-OS / Linux 软件仓库的协作关系
minimal_modules: library 与 projects 的分工
lectures.practice_task: 阅读 README.md 与 docs/index.rst，用一段话写出本仓库解决的三个具体问题；列出仓库顶层目录中哪些属于构建脚本、哪些属于源码或文档，并标注每个目录的作用。

lectures.title: 仓库与目录结构导览
lectures.topic: 系统讲解仓库顶层布局：library/、projects/、projects/scripts/、library/scripts/、docs/、scripts/ 各自承担的职责与内部组织规律。
learning_goals: 掌握 library 与 projects 目录的命名与组织规律
识别构建脚本（Makefile/Tcl）与设计源码（Verilog/VHDL）的位置
理解 projects/common 与 projects/<eval>/common 的区别
minimal_modules: library 与 projects 的子目录约定
lectures.practice_task: 浏览 library/ 与 projects/ 目录，挑选一个 library 模块和一个 project，分别记录其包含的文件类型（.v/.tcl/Makefile 等），并对比两者目录构成的异同。

lectures.title: 构建环境与工具链版本
lectures.topic: 讲解构建所需的 AMD Xilinx Vivado / Intel Quartus / Lattice Radiant 工具链、GNU Make，以及 scripts/adi_env.tcl 如何集中管理工具版本与环境变量。

理解 ADI_HDL_DIR、ADI_IGNORE_VERSION_CHECK 等关键环境变量

lectures.title: 构建第一个工程：从 make 到比特流
lectures.topic: 以 fmcomms2/zcu102 为例，演示 cd 到工程目录后执行 make 的完整入口流程，并理解 Makefile 如何声明库依赖并触发 Vivado。

lectures.title: 三层工程架构：载板 / 评估板 / 系统
lectures.topic: 依据官方 architecture.rst，讲解每个参考设计如何由 carrier 基设计、eval 基设计与系统特化设计三层叠加而成，以及 system_bd.tcl 如何依次 source 它们。
learning_goals: 理解载板（carrier-dependent）与评估板（carrier-independent）设计的分离

lectures.title: 单个工程的文件剖析
lectures.topic: 逐一讲解 Xilinx 工程的标准五件套：Makefile、system_project.tcl、system_bd.tcl、system_constr.xdc、system_top.v，以及它们之间的协作关系。
learning_goals: 理解 system_top.v 如何例化 system_wrapper 与 IO 缓冲

lectures.title: 文档体系导航
lectures.topic: 导览 docs/ 下的 Sphinx 文档结构：user_guide（架构/构建/移植/规范/发布）、library（各 IP 文档）、projects（参考设计清单）、regmap（寄存器表），并说明本地构建文档的方法。
